The Xyrauchen texanus, commonly known as the razorback sucker, hatches from a demersal, adhesive egg at a very small size; yolk-sac larvae emerge after a brief incubation period measuring only 0.8 centimeters  in total length at hatch. This minute size is typical of many catostomids and initiates a protracted growth trajectory. Field surveys of young-of-year indicate that the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0056 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0056 grams], a value inferred from the diameter of the yolked ovum. This extremely light birth mass imposes a high vulnerability to predation during the lecithotrophic larval stage, as the non-feeding larvae must rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until mouth opening. The initial growth phase under typical spring thermal regimes is rapid, with juveniles transitioning from yolk absorption to exogenous feeding within a few weeks. These early life stages are poorly sampled in the wild, but hatchery observations confirm that the minute hatchling length and negligible birth weight are consistent with the species' reproductive strategy of producing numerous, small offspring.

Adult Xyrauchen texanus exhibit pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a trait documented across much of their range in the Colorado River basin. Females attain a substantially larger maximum body size than males, with an ultimate total length for females reaching 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters]. In contrast, males are characteristically smaller, with the same measurement for males being approximately 90 centimeters [Li = approximately 90 centimeters], representing a modest but consistent reduction of roughly ten percent. These body sizes correspond to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 6000 grams [Wwi = approximately 6000 grams] for the largest recorded females, a mass that reflects the accumulation of lipid stores and gonadal tissue necessary for their high fecundity. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, observed in both wild and captive individuals maintained at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], is approximately 50 years [am = approximately 50 years]. This remarkably long lifespan positions the razorback sucker among the most long-lived of the North American catostomids.

Puberty in Xyrauchen texanus is a late-life event, consistent with its slow life-history strategy. Based on comparative data from related species such as Catostomus catostomus, the total length at puberty is estimated to be 54 centimeters [Lp = 54 centimeters]. This length corresponds to an age at sexual maturation of approximately 4 years after hatching when fish are reared at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], representing a time since birth at puberty of roughly 1460 days [tp = roughly 1460 days]. The delay in reproductive maturation is hypothesized to reflect the energetic demands of attaining a large body size in a relatively unproductive desert river system. Field collections have confirmed that individuals below this length threshold rarely exhibit gonadal recrudescence, supporting the use of this size-based metric as a reliable indicator of the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation in both sexes. The protracted juvenile phase is a critical period of vulnerability.

Reproductive output in the razorback sucker is correspondingly high once maturity is attained. Spawning occurs in aggregations over cobble or gravel substrates during late winter and early spring. Females are batch spawners, and at a body length of 35.6 centimeters, the estimated annual number of eggs produced amounts to approximately 103,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 103,000 eggs per spawning event], with a single spawning event occurring each year [F_R_i = single spawning event occurring each year] at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The relationship between body size and fecundity is strongly positive; larger females, approaching the ultimate length of 91 centimeters, can produce multiple batches of eggs totaling several hundred thousand ova per season. These high fecundities are necessary to offset extremely high early mortality rates.

Comparatively, the life-history traits of Xyrauchen texanus align with those of other large, long-lived freshwater fishes that exhibit an iteroparous strategy and high fecundity. In the context of a regulated river, the combination of a 50-year lifespan (approximately 50 years) [am = approximately 50 years] and a 4-year delay to maturity (roughly 4 years since birth) [tp = roughly 4 years since birth] means that reproductive value accumulates slowly, making the species particularly vulnerable to recruitment failure during extended periods of habitat degradation at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The substantial body size, with females reaching 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters] total length and an ultimate wet weight of approximately 6000 grams [Wwi = approximately 6000 grams], is among the highest recorded in the Catostomidae, reflecting an energy allocation toward bulk spawning biomass. These life-history parameters make the razorback sucker particularly susceptible to habitat alteration, especially the fragmentation of river systems that disrupts the spawning migrations of sexually mature adults. Conservation efforts focused on flow management and habitat connectivity are therefore directed toward protecting the adult population that accumulates reproductive value over many decades.
